lines: {target}? Gentle ground can make travelers careless.
Make sure travelers know this before visiting Meadow. Rest there, but do not forget night comes.
Flowers and bees do not bar the dark.
I'll remember Meadow as soft grass that still needs a lantern.
At the meadow, which risk looked small until you were standing beside it?
A tired traveler can mistake any path for home. How did you avoid that near the meadow?
Did anyone fall when loose stone on a steep slope turned worse?
How long could you travel once wind changing across the ridge set in?
I hope you filled every bottle before the meadow. Did you?
That trip makes a day in my little boat sound gentle.
Did you pack enough to share, or only enough to survive the trip?
Did wet, heat, or grit damage anything you depended on?
I hope your shelter had one good wall and no surprises.
Which traveler surprised you by staying calm near the meadow?
Could you smell the meadow before it came into view?
What looked harmless near the meadow until it began moving?
How many days passed before your legs forgave the journey?
Which mistake would you refuse to repeat near the meadow?
You came back changed, though perhaps only you can name how.
Do you think the place would feel different on a second visit?
{target}? Stone peaks make every fall honest.
Your best advice for Stony Peaks sounds simple. Bring blocks and stop before your legs shake.
Bare rock gives little cover and no softness.
I'll remember Stony Peaks as high stone with hard answers.
The first bad moment at the stony peaks must have changed the whole trip. What happened?
By the time you left the stony peaks, did you know the way or merely know what to avoid?
A person watches enemies and forgets the ground. Did the stony peaks punish that?
Did wind changing across the ridge follow you on the return trip?
How carefully did you ration water on the way to the stony peaks?
I would rather mend nets in rain than face a bad step with too much empty air below.
Did enough supper for the climb down last until you were safely headed home?
What did you leave behind because carrying it home was not worth the risk?
Shelter found after dark rarely feels as safe as it looks. How was yours?
A good companion notices fear without making a speech about it. Who noticed yours?
When wind hiding movement nearby changed, did you know why?
How near did the trouble come before anyone noticed it?
The return is where small injuries begin to matter. Who needed help?
Which lesson from that place belongs in every travel pack?
There is a part of that story you keep circling. You can leave it alone if you want.
If the choice were yours tomorrow, would you stay home?
{target}? Gravel moves when you most need it still.
I would tell anyone planning a trip to Windswept Gravelly Hills one thing. Test every slope before trusting it.
Loose stone tells lies under boots.
I will remember Windswept Gravelly Hills as windy hills that slide under pressure.
How quickly did trouble find you around the windswept gravelly hills?
Did the route home feel easier to recognize after everything you had seen?
Was the ground at the windswept gravelly hills harder on your legs or on your nerves?
Was there a safe place to wait out wind changing across the ridge?
The road home feels different when the water is gone. How close did you come?
Give me rough water over a bad step with too much empty air below any day.
How many meals did the journey take beyond what you expected?
Of everything you packed, what earned its place?
How many people shared the safest resting place near the windswept gravelly hills?
Someone must have kept you moving when home felt far away. Who was it?
Did the silence there feel peaceful, or did it feel watched?
When trouble reached the group, who spotted the safest opening?
What part of the return from the windswept gravelly hills felt longest?
What rule kept you alive once the original plan failed?
Thank you for trusting me with the part that was hardest to say.
Was one journey to the windswept gravelly hills enough for a lifetime?
{target}? Hard wind turns every edge into advice.
People setting out for Windswept Hills should remember this. Keep low and do not race the mountain.
Clouds move fast up there and so can mistakes.
I'll remember Windswept Hills as high rough land that talks in gusts.
Tell me when the windswept hills stopped feeling like an adventure and started feeling dangerous.
On the way toward the windswept hills, where did the route become difficult to read?
Could you move quickly over loose stone on a steep slope, or did caution win?
At the windswept hills, what sign told you the conditions were about to worsen?
Could you refill near the windswept hills, or only ration what you carried?
There are days I complain about the lake. Today will not be one of them.
A hungry traveler makes quick mistakes. Did your food hold out?
A spare tool is dead weight until the first one fails. Which spare saved you?
How did you locate the lee side of solid rock when everyone needed rest?
Who remembered the plan when trouble scattered everyone?
Were there moments at the windswept hills when hearing less felt worse?
Were you able to wait for danger to move, or did it force your hand?
Was the path home kinder than the one that took you out?
If you could change one choice from that trip, which would it be?
I can hear how tired you were, even now.
Tell that story by the fire sometime. Others need the honest version.
